mainTopic: Vows on a food and whether they include foods that come from it: milk and whey (קום), lentils and lentil cakes, gravy and meat sediment, and wine cooked into a dish.
overview: The גמרא opens by pointing out what looks like a contradiction in רבי יוסי's view. He forbids whey (קום) to someone who vowed off milk, yet he permits lentil cakes to someone who vowed off lentils. The answer is that vows follow local speech, and in רבי יוסי's town whey was called 'milk whey'. A ברייתא then teaches that a vow on a general food name does not reach related foods. A vow on a specific item, like 'this meat' or 'this wine', does reach its gravy, its sediment, or a dish that tastes of it. A new משנה rules that vowing off grapes or olives still allows wine and oil, but 'קונם these olives and grapes, that I will not taste' forbids them too. רמי בר חמא asks which words cause this: 'these' (אלו) or 'that I will not taste' (שאיני טועם). After several proofs are pushed away, the story of רבי טרפון and the eggs shows that 'these' is surely enough. A proof from the fish-brine משנה about 'that I will not taste' is rejected by רבא, so that half of the question is not resolved on this amud.

steps.title: רבי יוסי seems to contradict himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sets רבי יוסי's ruling on whey against his ruling on lentil cakes.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא raises a contradiction from another משנה: if someone vows off lentils, he is forbidden to eat lentil cakes, but רבי יוסי permits them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a later משנה where רבי יוסי is lenient. That seems to clash with his strict ruling about whey in our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In our משנה, רבי יוסי says a vow on milk also forbids קום, even though whey is a changed form of milk. With lentils he says the changed form (lentil cakes) is permitted. So does a changed form fall under the vow or not?

keyTerms.meaning: And we set them against each other: introduces a contradiction between two sources
Lentils
Cakes or a dish made from lentils
Permits

steps.confusionAlert: The contradiction is inside רבי יוסי's own views. It is not רבי יוסי against the רבנן. In the milk case he is the strict one, and in the lentil case he is the lenient one.

phrases.english: Gemara: And they raised a contradiction:
One who vows from lentils is forbidden in lentil cakes,
and Rabbi Yosei permits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה's dispute about milk and whey.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי's ruling in the משנה that a vow on milk forbids קום.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a changed form of a food is included in the vow (whey), then lentil cakes should be included too. רבי יוסי permits them, so his two rulings seem inconsistent.

steps.title: Each ruling follows local speech
steps.stepSummary: There is no contradiction, because vows follow the local way of talking, and in רבי יוסי's town whey was called 'milk whey'.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. Each Sage ruled according to his own place. Where the רבנן lived, people called milk 'milk' and whey 'whey'. Where רבי יוסי lived, people also called whey 'milk whey'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יוסי has no general rule about changed foods. He simply followed how people in his place used the word 'milk'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vows are understood by what the words mean to the people saying them. In רבי יוסי's town, whey carried the name 'milk', so a vow on 'milk' covered it. Lentil cakes were not called 'lentils', so they stay permitted, and his views no longer clash.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult: the contradiction is resolved
Each Sage according to his own place
Whey, the liquid left over from milk
They call

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a basic rule of נדרים: the meaning of a vow depends on how people speak where it was made.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:

phrases.aramaic: מָר כִּי אַתְרֵיהּ וּמָר כִּי אַתְרֵיהּ.
phrases.english: This Sage according to his place, and that Sage according to his place.
In the place of the Rabbis
they call milk 'milk' and whey 'whey',
in the place of Rabbi Yosei
they also call whey 'milk whey'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Local custom distinction: the rulings depend on local language, not on a general principle.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רבי יוסי holds that a changed form of a food is always included in a vow on that food.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוסי included whey only because in his town it was called 'milk whey'. Changed foods without the name, like lentil cakes, are not included.
steps.whatToRemember: A vow follows local speech. Whey falls under a vow on 'milk' only where people call it by milk's name.

steps.title: A ברייתא on related foods and a specific piece of meat
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that a vow on one food name does not include related foods, but a vow on 'this meat' includes its gravy and sediment.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: One who vows off milk may have whey, and one who vows off whey may have milk. One who vows off milk may have cheese, and one who vows off cheese may have milk. One who vows off gravy may have meat sediment, and one who vows off sediment may have gravy. If he said 'This meat is forbidden to me', he is forbidden in it, its gravy, and its sediment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that lists pairs of related foods that do not forbid each other. It then gives one case where the vow does reach the related foods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the vow is on a general name like 'milk' or 'gravy', only that name is forbidden, so related foods stay permitted. This matches the רבנן's view on whey. When he points at a specific piece, 'this meat', the vow is on the item itself, so whatever came out of it (its gravy and sediment) is forbidden too.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught: introduces a ברייתא
One who vows
Cheese
Gravy, the liquid of cooked meat
Sediment or bits of meat left at the bottom of the pot

phrases.english: It was taught: One who vows from milk
is permitted in whey,
from whey, he is permitted in milk.
From milk, he is permitted in cheese,
from cheese, he is permitted in milk.
From gravy, he is permitted in sediment,
from sediment, he is permitted in gravy.
If he said 'This meat is upon me',
phrases.notes: 'Upon me' means forbidden to me. The key word is 'this': he is pointing at one specific piece.

phrases.english: he is forbidden in it, in its gravy, and in its sediment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that follows the רבנן's standard view that whey is separate from milk, and adds related cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow on a general food name does not forbid related foods made from it. A vow on a specific item forbids that item together with its gravy and sediment.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two kinds of vows. 'Meat' or 'gravy' as a general name stays narrow. 'This meat' targets one object, so it reaches everything that came out of it.

steps.title: Wine cooked into a dish
steps.stepSummary: A general vow on wine allows a dish that only tastes of wine. A vow on 'this wine' forbids a dish it fell into if the wine's taste can be felt.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who vows off wine is permitted to eat a cooked dish that has the taste of wine. If he said 'This wine is קונם for me, that I will not taste it', and it fell into a cooked dish, then if the dish has the taste of wine, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with the same pattern for wine: a general vow versus a vow on a specific wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A general vow on 'wine' covers what people call wine, and a cooked dish is not called wine, so the dish is permitted. When he forbids 'this wine', that actual wine is forbidden. If it gives the dish its taste, the forbidden wine is present in the dish, so the dish becomes forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: A cooked dish
Taste or flavor
A word used for making a vow, standing in for 'like a קרבן'
Taste

steps.whatToRemember: A vow on a general name covers only what carries that name. A vow on a specific item ('this meat', 'this wine') follows the item wherever it goes, even into gravy or into a dish where its taste is felt.

phrases.english: One who vows from wine

phrases.aramaic: מוּתָּר בְּתַבְשִׁיל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ טַעַם יַיִן.
phrases.english: is permitted in a cooked dish that has the taste of wine.
If he said: 'This wine is konam, that I will not taste it'
and it fell into the cooked dish,

phrases.aramaic: אִם יֵשׁ בּוֹ טַעַם יַיִן — הֲרֵי זֶה אָסוּר.
phrases.english: if it has the taste of wine, it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, applying the general-name versus specific-item pattern to wine.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general vow on wine permits a dish with wine's taste. A vow on specific wine forbids a dish it fell into if its taste is felt.

steps.title: Vowing off grapes and olives, and what comes out of them
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה teaches that a vow against grapes does not forbid wine, and a vow against olives does not forbid oil. But 'קונם these olives and grapes, that I will not taste' forbids the fruit and its juice or oil.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who vows off grapes may still drink wine. One who vows off olives may still use olive oil. But if he said, 'These olives and grapes are קונם, that I will not taste them,' he is forbidden in the fruit itself and in what comes out of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new משנה. It gives two lenient cases and then one strict case about the juice or oil that comes out of fruit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wine and oil have their own names, so a vow on 'grapes' or 'olives' does not cover them. The strict case uses special wording: 'these' and 'that I will not taste'. With that wording, the vow does reach the wine and oil.

keyTerms.meaning: One who makes a נדר (vow)
A substitute word for קרבן, used to forbid something by a vow
What comes out of them, such as wine from grapes or oil from olives
Forbidden / permitted

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who vows off grapes
is permitted to drink wine.
One who vows off olives is permitted to use oil.
If he said: "Olives and grapes are קונם,
phrases.notes: קונם works like the word קרבן. Saying it makes the food forbidden to him like a holy offering.

phrases.english: these, that I will not taste"
he is forbidden in them and in what comes out of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. It follows the same idea as step 4: a general vow is lenient, while a specific vow reaches further.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow on grapes or olives does not forbid wine or oil. 'קונם these olives and grapes, that I will not taste' forbids both the fruit and what comes out of it.

steps.title: Which words in the vow make it strict?
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא asks whether the strict ruling comes from the word 'these' or from the words 'that I will not taste'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא asked: Is it the word 'these' that matters, or is it the words 'that I will not taste'?
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא asks what exactly in the last case of the משנה causes the strict ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The strict vow uses two special phrases. 'These' points to specific fruit. 'That I will not taste' speaks about tasting, and the taste of the fruit is in its juice too. We need to know which phrase causes the juice and oil to be forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: He asks, raising an open question
Specifically; exactly this and nothing else
That I will not taste

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rami bar Ḥama asks:
Is it specifically because he said "these,"
or specifically because he said "that I will not taste"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the wording of the strict case in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the vow reach the wine and oil because of 'these' or because of 'that I will not taste'?

steps.title: A try to answer from the wording of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that if 'these' were the key word, the משנה would not need to add 'that I will not taste'. So maybe 'that I will not taste' is what matters.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think 'these' is what matters, why does the משנה need the words 'that I will not taste'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer רמי בר חמא's question from the wording of the משנה itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that every word in a משנה is there for a reason. If 'these' alone were enough, the words 'that I will not taste' would be extra. That would suggest those words are the real cause.

keyTerms.meaning: If it enters your mind; if you were to think
Why do I need it? (asks why a word or detail is there)

phrases.english: If it enters your mind that it is specifically because of "these,"
why do I need "that I will not taste"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That 'that I will not taste' is the cause of the strict ruling.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The wording of the משנה, which would have extra words if 'these' alone were enough.

steps.title: The extra words still teach something
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes the proof away. The words 'that I will not taste' are there to teach that even with them, the vow is strict only if he also said 'these'.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the משנה is teaching: even though he said 'that I will not taste', he is forbidden only if he also said 'these'. If he did not say 'these', he is not forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 7. The words 'that I will not taste' can have their own purpose even if 'these' is the key word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה may include 'that I will not taste' to show that those words are not enough by themselves. Only adding 'these' makes the vow reach the wine and oil. So the wording of the משנה does not settle the question either way.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us
He becomes forbidden

steps.confusionAlert: This does not prove that 'these' is the key word. It only shows that the משנה's wording fits that view too, so the question is not settled here. Step 13 brings a proof about 'these', and step 14 narrows the question.

phrases.english: This is what it teaches us:
that even though he said "that I will not taste,"
if he said "these" he is forbidden,
and if not, he is not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the attempted proof in step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from the wording of the משנה. It does not answer the question itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The words 'that I will not taste' are not extra. They can teach that those words alone are not enough without 'these'.

steps.title: רבא's proof from another משנה
steps.stepSummary: רבא brings a later משנה. Saying 'these fruits are קונם' forbids their replacements and what grows from them, which suggests that what comes out of them stays permitted. So 'these' alone does not forbid juice or oil.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Come and hear. If someone says, 'These fruits are קונם upon me,' or 'They are קונם to my mouth,' he is forbidden in what is traded for them and in what grows from them. That suggests he is permitted in what comes out of them!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא tries to answer רמי בר חמא's question using a different משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: That משנה uses the word 'these' but does not mention what comes out of the fruit. So the juice must be permitted. If 'these' alone does not forbid the juice, then in our משנה the cause must be 'that I will not taste'.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear; introduces a proof from a source
Their replacements; things traded in exchange for them
What grows from them

steps.whyThisMatters: If this proof holds, the deciding factor is the language of tasting, not the word 'these'.

phrases.english: Rava said: Come and hear:
"These fruits are קונם upon me,"
or "They are קונם to my mouth"
he is forbidden in their replacements and in what grows from them,
which implies that what comes out of them is permitted!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from our משנה was rejected, רבא brings a new proof from a different משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That 'these' alone does not forbid what comes out of the fruit, so 'that I will not taste' is the deciding phrase.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A later משנה: 'These fruits are קונם upon me' forbids replacements and what grows from them, but not what comes out of them.

steps.title: The משנה only skipped juice because it wanted to teach a bigger point
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רבא's proof. Juice coming out of the fruit really is forbidden too. The משנה just chose to teach the bigger news that replacements are forbidden like things that grow from the fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, the same law applies: even what comes out of them is forbidden. The משנה preferred to teach us that their replacements are treated like what grows from them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away רבא's proof from step 9. Not mentioning juice does not mean juice is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא reasoned from silence: the משנה lists replacements and growths but not juice, so juice must be permitted. The answer is that juice is obviously forbidden. The משנה used its words on the surprising point instead: replacements contain nothing of the original fruit, yet they are still forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: the same law applies
what comes out of them (juice, oil)
their replacements (things traded for them)
what grows from them
it is better for it (to teach)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read silence as permission here. The גמרא says the משנה left juice out because it was obvious, not because juice is allowed.

phrases.aramaic: הוּא הַדִּין דַּאֲפִילּוּ בְּיוֹצֵא מֵהֶן אָסוּר.
phrases.english: The same law applies: even what comes out of them is forbidden.
But it was better for the משנה to teach us this:
that their replacements are just like what grows from them.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא הַדִּין דַּאֲפִילּוּ בְּיוֹצֵא מֵהֶן אָסוּר
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the inference that juice is permitted because the משנה did not list it.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה left juice out because it preferred to teach the bigger news about replacements, not because juice is permitted.

steps.title: A second proof from the end of the same משנה
steps.stepSummary: The same משנה says that with 'that I will not eat' or 'that I will not taste', he may have the replacements and what grows from them. That suggests what comes out of them is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If he said 'that I will not eat' or 'that I will not taste', he is permitted to have their replacements and what grows from them. That implies what comes out of them is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new proof from the next part of the same משנה, aimed at the phrase 'that I will not taste'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case the משנה permits only replacements and growths, and it does not say juice is permitted. The inference is that juice stays forbidden. If so, the phrase 'that I will not taste' seems to be what forbids the juice.

keyTerms.meaning: come and hear (introduces a proof)
that I will not eat
this implies (introduces an inference)

phrases.english: Come and hear: if he said 'that I will not eat' or 'that I will not taste' —
he is permitted to have their replacements and what grows from them.
This implies that what comes out of them is forbidden!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: שֶׁאֵינִי אוֹכֵל, וְשֶׁאֵינִי טוֹעֵם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New attempt at a proof after step 10 pushed away the last one
steps.raayaObject: That 'that I will not taste' forbids the juice that comes out of the fruit
steps.raayaSupportSource: The second half of the משנה about 'these fruits are קונם'

steps.title: The משנה just kept both halves the same
steps.stepSummary: The proof fails. The first half did not mention juice, so the second half left it out too, just to match. Nothing can be learned from the silence.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the first part did not mention 'what comes out of them', the last part did not mention it either.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof in step 11 by explaining why juice is missing from the second half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The missing juice in the second half is just a matter of matching the style of the first half. It tells us nothing about whether juice is forbidden or permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: since, because of (the first part)
took, mentioned
the first part
the last part

phrases.english: Since it did not mention 'what comes out of them' in the first part,
it also did not mention 'what comes out of them' in the last part.

steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the inference from the second half of the משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The silence about juice comes from matching the first half's wording, so no inference can be drawn from it.

steps.title: רבי טרפון's eggs prove that 'this' forbids the flavor that comes out
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה reports that רבי טרפון forbade him eggs cooked with meat he had vowed against. The חכמים say this applies only when he said 'this meat', because a vowed food that gives flavor to a mixture makes the mixture forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי יהודה said: Once רבי טרפון forbade me eggs that were cooked with it. They said to him: When is that? When he said 'this meat is forbidden to me'. Someone who vows against a thing, and it gets mixed into something else and gives it flavor, that mixture is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof from an earlier משנה. Pointing at a specific food ('this') makes even what comes out of it, like its flavor, forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The flavor that passes from the meat into the eggs is like juice coming out of fruit. The חכמים say this is forbidden only when he said 'this meat'. So a word pointing at specific food, like 'this' or 'these', is enough to forbid what comes out of it.

keyTerms.meaning: an incident that happened
when (does this apply)?
got mixed
gives flavor (the forbidden food can be tasted in the mix)

steps.whyThisMatters: This proof answers the half of the question about 'these', and that is why the גמרא reshapes the question in the next step.

phrases.english: Come and hear: רבי יהודה said:
It once happened that רבי טרפון forbade me
eggs that were cooked with it.
phrases.notes: 'It' is the meat. In that משנה the person had vowed against meat.

phrases.english: They said to him: When is that so?
When he said 'this meat is forbidden to me'.
Because when someone vows against a thing and it gets mixed into another food,

phrases.aramaic: וְיֵשׁ בּוֹ בְּנוֹתֵן טַעַם — הֲרֵי זֶה אָסוּר.
phrases.english: and there is enough of it to give flavor, the mixture is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: מַעֲשֶׂה וְאָסַר רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third attempt at a proof, from a different משנה
steps.raayaObject: That the word 'this' or 'these' on its own forbids what comes out of the food
steps.raayaSupportSource: The earlier משנה about רבי טרפון and eggs cooked with meat

steps.title: The question is reshaped: only 'that I will not taste' is in doubt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts that 'these' surely forbids the juice. The real question is whether 'that I will not taste' also does this on its own.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have no question about 'these'. It definitely works. Our question is about 'that I will not taste': does it count on its own or not?
steps.whatsHappening: Because of the proof in step 13, the גמרא narrows רמי בר חמא's question. 'These' is settled, and only 'that I will not taste' is still open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The original question asked which of the two wordings causes the strict ruling. Now 'these' is known to work. What is still unknown is whether 'that I will not taste' is enough by itself to forbid the juice.

keyTerms.meaning: we are unsure about, our question is
exactly, specifically (it really counts)
not exactly (it does not count on its own)

steps.whatToRemember: 'These' (אלו) definitely forbids juice and oil. The open question is only whether 'that I will not taste' (שאיני טועם) also does this.

phrases.aramaic: בְּ״אֵלּוּ״ — לָא קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לַן דְּדַוְקָא הוּא.
phrases.english: About 'these' we have no question, since it certainly counts.
Our question is about 'that I will not taste':
does it count on its own, or not?
phrases.notes: Does 'that I will not taste' by itself forbid the juice, or is it not enough on its own?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּאֵלּוּ לָא קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לַן דְּדַוְקָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the proof of step 13 and narrows the question from step 6
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the phrase 'that I will not taste' on its own forbids the juice and oil that come out of the fruit

steps.title: Proof from the fish vow: brine is allowed
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says that someone who vows 'fish, that I will not taste' is forbidden in all fish but allowed to have minced sardines and fish brine. So 'that I will not taste' does not seem to forbid what comes out of the fish.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If someone says 'Fish, fishes, that I will not taste,' he is forbidden to eat any of them, large or small, raw or cooked. But he is allowed to have minced sardines and fish brine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof from a משנה to answer the question from step 14. That question was whether 'שאיני טועם' by itself forbids what comes out of the food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fish brine (ציר) is liquid that comes out of fish. The person said 'that I will not taste', and the משנה still lets him have the brine. So it looks like this wording does not forbid what comes out of the food.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear. The גמרא is about to bring a source as a proof.
That I will not taste. This is the vow wording being tested.
Minced or mashed sardines, a small kind of fish.
Fish brine, the liquid that comes out of fish.

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'חַיִּים' does not mean 'living fish'. It means raw, the opposite of cooked.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
'Fish, fishes, that I will not taste'
he is forbidden in them,
whether large or small,
whether raw or cooked,
and he is permitted in minced sardines and in fish brine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question raised in step 14 about 'שאיני טועם'.
steps.raayaObject: Whether 'that I will not taste' on its own forbids what comes out of the vowed food.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about vowing off fish, which allows fish brine.

steps.title: The brine had already come out before the vow
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the proof. The משנה may be talking about brine that had already come out of the fish before the person made his נדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The משנה means brine that had already come out of the fish before the vow.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא knocks down the proof from step 15.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the brine was already separate when he made the נדר, it was never part of the fish he vowed against. So the משנה only shows that brine that came out earlier is allowed. It tells us nothing about juice that comes out of the fish after the vow.

keyTerms.meaning: It had already come out of them, meaning before the vow was made.

steps.whatToRemember: The fish-brine proof fails, because that brine may have come out before the vow. So at the end of this amud, the question from step 14 about 'שאיני טועם' is still not settled.

phrases.english: רבא said:
And it had already come out of them.
phrases.notes: He means the brine came out of the fish before the person made his vow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 15.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the fish brine in the משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the brine came out after the vow. It could be brine that had already come out before the vow, so it was never covered by the vow at all.
